name: Essays, Resumes, and Interviews
title: Essays, Resumes, and Interviews
answer: AI can help students brainstorm college essays, organize ideas, and practice resumes and interviews, but it must never write the essay or replace the student's own voice. Schools need clear rules because AI-written essays show nothing about the student and may break a college's rules, and because some students become passive when AI does too much of the work.

sections.body: This idea covers how AI should and should not be used in three parts of the college and career process: essays, resumes, and interviews. A college essay is meant to reveal who the student is, and an AI-written essay reveals nothing about them while possibly violating a college's rules. The solution is a configured tool, such as Gemini for Education with hint only instructions, that asks students questions to prompt brainstorming and reflection rather than producing text. The tool never writes the essay, so the thinking and the writing stay with the student. The same principle applies to resumes and mock interviews, where AI can support practice but must not take over the student's choices.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, counselors and teachers first make the rules clear to students. Students may use AI to brainstorm topics, organize ideas, or get feedback on a draft they wrote themselves, but they may not submit AI-written text as their own. Because many colleges now state their own policies on AI use in applications, students should check those policies. In high school English units, students used AI to build resumes and practice text based interviews, which gave them useful practice with some risks attached. Teachers should build in steps that require students to make their own choices and explain them, so the work stays theirs.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea's evidence through a study it cites. In high school English units that used AI to help students build resumes and practice text based interviews, many students questioned and improved the AI's suggestions, but others became passive and relied on it too much (Kwon et al., 2026). Students also noticed that AI responses could be generic. The text reports no other study, figure, or finding for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set out plainly. An AI-written essay shows nothing about the student and may violate a college's rules, so the tool must never write the essay. Students cannot submit text written by AI as their own, and they should check the policies many colleges now state on AI use in applications. The risk in resume and interview practice is passivity, since some students relied on the AI too much, and generic AI responses. The decisions stay with the student and the teacher: teachers should build in steps that require students to make their own choices and explain them.
